questions.q: What is the core structural difference between GARCH and stochastic volatility (SV) models?
options: GARCH can only be used for daily data, while SV works on any frequency
In GARCH, conditional variance is a deterministic function of past data; in SV, volatility follows its own separate random process
SV models do not allow volatility to change over time at all
GARCH requires intraday data, while SV never does
questions.explain: GARCH's variance equation is fully determined by observed past shocks and variance, with no new randomness entering it. SV models instead let volatility evolve according to its own stochastic process driven by a separate, independent shock.

questions.q: In the canonical discrete-time SV model r_t = sigma_t * z_t with log(sigma_t^2) following its own AR(1)-like process driven by eta_t, why is volatility called a 'latent variable'?
options: Because sigma_t is printed directly in the dataset
Because sigma_t is never directly observed, even given the complete history of returns — it must be inferred
Because z_t and eta_t are always equal to each other
Because latent variables only appear in GARCH models
questions.explain: Unlike GARCH's exactly computable sigma_t^2, the SV model's volatility process is driven by its own unobserved innovation eta_t, so its true current value can never be computed exactly from the data — only inferred with uncertainty.

questions.q: Why is maximum likelihood estimation straightforward for GARCH but not for stochastic volatility models?
options: GARCH models have no likelihood function at all
GARCH's variance is an exact function of observed past data, while SV's likelihood requires integrating over all possible latent volatility paths
SV models have fewer parameters than GARCH, making estimation trivial
Maximum likelihood cannot be used for any volatility model
questions.explain: Because GARCH's conditional variance is fully determined by observed data, its likelihood is directly computable. SV's likelihood requires integrating over the unobserved volatility path, a much harder computational problem typically solved with particle filters or MCMC instead.

questions.q: Which two estimation approaches are mentioned as standard ways to fit stochastic volatility models in practice?
options: Ordinary least squares and simple linear regression
Particle filters and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods
The Ljung-Box test and the ADF test
Grid search over AIC and BIC
questions.explain: Particle filters (sequential Monte Carlo methods) and MCMC (Bayesian sampling approaches) are the standard tools for estimating SV models, since neither offers a simple closed-form likelihood the way GARCH does.

questions.q: What is the Heston model, and why is it notable in options pricing?
options: A discrete-time GARCH variant used only for interest rate data
A continuous-time stochastic volatility model that can reproduce the volatility smile that a constant-volatility (Black-Scholes) model cannot
A statistical test for volatility clustering
An alternative name for the GJR-GARCH model
questions.explain: The Heston model is a continuous-time SV model where both the asset price and its variance follow coupled stochastic differential equations. It's popular in options pricing because, unlike Black-Scholes' constant-volatility assumption, it can reproduce the volatility smile seen in real options markets.
